editorial.headline: Wholesale Trade in Blank and Removable Media: Open Nationally, Blocked in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This activity is nationally open to full foreign ownership, yet PMA registration in Bali is blocked under the province-wide risk-based moratorium.
editorial.body:
A business under this activity trades wholesale in diskettes, removable disks and flash drives, blank audio and video tapes, and blank CDs and DVDs. The scope is specific: it is about the wholesale circulation of unused storage and recording media, from legacy formats to removable digital media. It is not framed as a retail activity, a content business, or a manufacturing operation; its commercial centre of gravity is the wholesale trade in these blank and removable media products.

The activity is open across every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. Nationally, it is classified as TERBUKA for foreign investment, with a maximum foreign ownership allowance of 100%. In practical terms, the national investment position is unambiguous: a foreign investor may hold the entire business, subject to the activity being registered within this stated scope and at one of the listed scales.

Bali tells a different story. A foreigner cannot register this activity in Bali today. The Bali classification is Blocked (risk class), and the record identifies the reason directly: at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope, bringing the activity within Bali’s moratorium from 13 May 2026. The provincial rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities for PMA, island-wide and permanently.

That produces a clear distinction that founders should not blur. The national foreign-ownership ceiling remains 100%; it has not been replaced by a lower Bali ownership percentage. But a full national foreign-ownership allowance does not create a Bali registration route where the provincial PMA block applies. For this wholesale activity, the national framework says foreign investment is open, while Bali’s risk-based moratorium prevents PMA registration on the island. The relevant question is therefore not how much foreign ownership is permitted nationally, but whether the intended Bali registration is available at all. On the record provided, it is not.
